content.title: Personal Branding 101: Your Guide to Building a Lasting Brand
content.text: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeIsaac Mashman, Denver, CO 2024 by Wiechman MediaWhat Is Personal Branding, Really?Personal branding isn’t just a buzzword or a fancy Instagram bio — it’s you. It’s every single thing about you: your passions, hobbies, flaws, faith, political leanings, even your eye color. From the class clown in school to the CEO in the boardroom, you’ve had a personal brand your entire life, whether you knew it or not. The term was coined by Tom Peters in 1997 in his Fast Company article “The Brand Called You,” aimed at C-suite execs, but it’s since exploded into a cultural phenomenon, thanks to leaders like Gary Vaynerchuk and the rise of the internet.Here’s the thing…Personal branding isn’t new. Think about Adam and Eve, King Hammurabi, or Alexander the Great. They weren’t posting on X, but they had reputations — personal brands — built on their actions and how others perceived them. Your personal brand exists because you’re a thinking, living human. It’s not tied to social media or tech; if the internet vanished tomorrow, I could still walk into my local Chamber of Commerce and be Isaac Mashman. Your personal brand is essentially the legacy created by your actions; a collection of everything you do, big or small, and it’s something you can consciously direct to achieve your ambitions.Why Build Your Personal Brand? The Big Three MotivatorsSo, why put in the effort to grow your personal brand? It’s not about boredom or chasing likes — it’s about ambition. I’ve concluded in my experience and observation that it boils down to three core reasons that drive people, and honestly, reflects what we want out of life: money, mission, and vanity.Money: Building a personal brand can open doors to revenue. A business owner might position themselves as a public figure to charge premium rates or land sponsorships. A comedian could go from local gigs to selling out Madison Square Garden. An employee might climb the corporate ladder or negotiate a higher salary. With 4 billion people online globally, promoting yourself costs nothing but time, and the potential is endless.Mission: Some are driven by a cause. Maybe you’re a victim of abuse turning pain into power, like Les Brown did with his stutter, becoming a renowned speaker. Or you’re passionate about saving animals or promoting eco-conscious choices. Your personal brand amplifies your message and impact.Vanity: Let’s be real — attention feels good. Some build their brand to be known, like musicians filling arenas or stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Vanity alone can veer into narcissism, but paired with money or mission, it’s a healthy motivator.Take a minute to ask: why are you building your brand? Money, mission, vanity — or a mix? Knowing your “why” keeps you grounded through burnout or flops. It’s your fuel for the long haul.The Four Pillar Questions: Your Personal Branding BlueprintTo build a brand that lasts, you need clarity. In my book, I lay out the Four Pillar Questions to guide you. Grab a pen and paper — old-school style — and answer these:Why are you building your personal brand?You’ve got your money, mission, or vanity answer from above. Be specific.What do you want to be known for?Fast-forward 20 years. Are you the motivational speaker who changed lives? The entrepreneur who boosted company revenue by 1,000%? The advocate who saved a species? Also, what don’t you want to be known for? I run from pay-to-play press or shady tactics to stay within my individual morals.Who are you?This is about self-awareness. List your hobbies, interests, beliefs, and quirks. Ask friends or family, “What do you think of when you think of me?” Clarity here shapes your personal brand’s genuineness.How do you get to where you want to be?This isn’t about Instagram hacks (plenty of resources for that). It’s about strategy — building credibility, relationships, and rapport over time.These questions aren’t fluff. Answering them gives you the fledgling of a roadmap to align your actions with your goals, whether you’re a chiropractor, a CEO, or a creator.The Four Laws of Personal Branding: Your Guiding PrinciplesJust like Newton’s laws of physics, I’ve developed the Four Laws of Personal Branding — a proclamation of depth, progression, and scale. These laws govern how brands grow and thrive:Law of Familiarity: The more someone encounters you — on social media, email, or in person — the more they trust you. Think of your first day at school: strangers became friends through repeated exposure. Show up consistently to occupy mindspace.Law of Connection: People crave relatability. Share your coffee addiction, your love for biking, or your struggles to build rapport. Without familiarity, connection can’t happen, but together, they create trust.Law of Fame and Influence: Fame (awareness) and influence (action) are symbiotic. In 2019, an influencer with millions of followers flopped an apparel line because she had fame but no influence. Connection drives influence, not just eyeballs.Law of Personal Branding: Your brand is born with you and can’t be destroyed, even by death — but it can be forgotten. A Mesopotamian farmer’s impact lived on, though nameless. Your actions today shape a legacy written by others, not you.These laws show that branding isn’t random. Familiarity leads to connection, which fuels influence, creating a lasting brand.Why People Consume Your Content: The Four ReasonsEver wonder why someone stops scrolling to watch your video or pay for your content? There are four reasons people engage, and understanding them makes you a better creator:Education: They learn something — skills, hacks, or perspectives. From fixing a sink on YouTube to mastering a business strategy, content that teaches sticks.Entertainment: People want to laugh, cry, or escape. Comedians nail this, but business content can blend humor to avoid being dry. (No one wants a boring lecture on personal branding laws, right?)Inspiration/Motivation: Your content sparks a desire for more — think a Rolls-Royce lifestyle or a backyard makeover. Inspiration is the feeling; motivation drives action.Connection: People follow to feel close to you. When I share my love for coffee or stories about my grandfather, it builds rapport. Subconscious or not, connection keeps them coming back.Pro tip: Benchmark the content you consume. Why do you watch certain creators? Is it lively or dull? Use those insights to craft content that hits all four — educate, entertain, inspire, and connect — for a loyal audience.Personal Brand vs. Reputation: What’s the Difference?Your personal brand is you — everything from your hobbies to your hustle. Your reputation, though, is what people say about you when you’re not around. It’s how they feel when your name pops up. Think of John, always late to meetings. His coworkers might say, “Don’t rush, he’s late anyway,” signaling he doesn’t respect time. That’s his reputation.Get Isaac Mashman’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.Remember me for faster sign inReputation ties to authority — the trust you earn through competence. Doctors have it from years of training; you build it with content, speaking, or testimonials. But it’s fragile. One bad move — like a pastor partying despite preaching conservative values — can tank it. I liken it to an oak tree: 100 years to grow, an hour to chop down. Avoid “guilty by association” risks (e.g., photos with controversial figures) and stay vigilant. Research who you align with, from interviewees to publications, to protect your hard-earned rep.Identity Positioning: My Proprietary StrategyToo many “experts” push growth hacks that miss the mark. Personal branding is about person and brand. The person is your quirks. The brand is your profession — what you do for money or impact. Most online coaches scream, “I help you scale to $30k in 90 days!” but skip the personal hook that builds rapport.That’s why I developed Identity Positioning, introduced in my 2024 paper Identity Positioning: A Macroscopic View on Personal Branding. It combines a personal hook (who you are) with a professional punchline (what you do). Share your struggles or hobbies to spark interest, then deliver value to keep them. This holistic approach ensures people connect with you as a human, not just a service, giving them a reason to stay.Final Thoughts: Build Your Brand with IntentionPersonal branding isn’t about chasing followers or faking expertise — it’s about directing your legacy with purpose. Whether driven by money, mission, or vanity, use the Four Pillar Questions to clarify your path, the Four Laws to guide your growth, and Identity Positioning to stand out. Protect your reputation like an oak tree, and create content that educates, entertains, inspires, and connects.Ready to dive deeper? Grab Personal Branding: A Manifesto on Fame and Influence on Amazon for the full philosophy, or reach out to Mashman Consulting Group to optimize your brand. I encourage you to build something unforgettable, go out and make it happen, or don’t. The decision is yours.
